articles.title: Libreboot 26.10 "Ominous Olive" released with UEFI, Chromebook support
articles.content: Return to index Article published by: Leah Rowe Date of publication: 15 October 2026 You can find today’s release in https://rsync.libreboot.org/stable/26.10/ or you can use one of the mirrors . Libreboot is free, open source boot firmware replacing proprietary BIOS/UEFI firmware on supported Intel/AMD and ARM64 hardware. It initialises the hardware inside your computer such as the CPU or memory controller, configuring the machine in such a way as to enable use of an operating system like Linux or BSD at boot - and now Microsoft Windows is also compatible because Libreboot has added full UEFI support via MrChromebox EDK2 payload. Libreboot offers greater security and customisation compared to proprietary firmware; its goal, plainly, is to rid the world of proprietary software and to do that, we therefore try to provide firmware that is extremely easy for non-technical users to understand. Today’s release changelog is relative to the previous Libreboot 26.01 release. This is a very special release, with several major design changes made regardless of hardware changes, so users should read this changelog very carefully - and read it twice. First thing’s first. (and yes, you read the previous paragraph correctly) A strongly anti-AI policy was added to a new file: AGENTS.md in lbmk. This is the most important change in the release. Now everything else: WARNING: MAJOR design changes were made to this release, in ways that may affect lots of existing setups. We now use EDK2 as the default payload, with GRUB/SeaBIOS provided in flash as EFI builds for backward compatibility. Everything works, but there are some caveats so please read this release changelog very carefully. The first major change is: 233 Intel/AMD Chromebooks added [link] The full list of boards is quite long, so it’s shown at the end of this article. All 233 of them! MrChromebox supports nearly every Chromebook, and this release imports all boards from that project. This includes everything up to the most recent Intel and AMD hardware. Imported all 233 currently supported Chromebooks from the MrChromebox coreboot distro. Baytrail (Kip) tested - others need testing. Source-only in this release (must build from source, no binaries provided). This was done with a utility I wrote at util/mrimport/ which generates configs for lbmk, including revisions and submodules. I made further tweaks manually; further updates upstream can be synced in Libreboot by diffing again the output of mrimport between revisions, adapted into Libreboot irrespective of the latter’s modifications which are numerous - and will be covered next. articles.title: Muse Spark Open
articles.content: Muse Spark Open is available today and brings leading agentic capabilities to your desktop for the first time on Apple M5 Ultra Mac Studios. Today, we’re releasing the weights for Muse Spark Open, the most capable US open-weight model to date. Muse Spark Open is a natively multimodal model with 816B total parameters (42B active) and a 1M-token context window. Built for coding and agentic work, it excels at long-horizon tasks, complex software engineering, and multi-step reasoning. We believe the future is for everyone , and that includes the freedom to run advanced models wherever, including at home. Muse Spark Open is the first model in its class to run on your desktop using two Apple M5 Ultra Mac Studios with the latest MLX framework. Muse Spark Open is available today through API platforms at Baseten, Fireworks AI, Groq, Modal, Nebius, OpenRouter and Together AI. Model weights are available for download on Amazon SageMaker AI, Google Cloud Model Garden, Hugging Face, and Microsoft Foundry Models. It runs on leading inference engines like SGLang, vLLM, TensorRT-LLM, Hugging Face Transformers, Apple MLX, llama.cpp, and Unsloth with optimizations for AMD, Apple, Intel, and NVIDIA silicon. Developers can easily further customize the model using the PyTorch framework. Key Benchmarks For more details about our evaluations, see the evaluation methodology report . Optimized for Apple Silicon Leveraging the latest version of MLX, Muse Spark Open was optimized to run on Mac Studio with M5 Ultra, and together they’re the best way to run a powerful model on your own desktop. Apple’s unified memory architecture lets the M5 Ultra's integrated GPU use up to 512 GB per Mac Studio, so two machines can hold an entire model. And the chip’s 1.2 TB/s of memory bandwidth is fast enough to read the small slice each token needs. The result is two Mac Studios behave like one supercomputer with a terabyte of unified memory. We tested a range of agentic workflows running entirely on-device, using Muse Code powered by Muse Spark Open, including shipping real iOS changes to Ice Cubes (an open-source Mastodon client) — bug fixes, new features, full build — and driving DaVinci Resolve end to end, with the model reviewing footage frame by frame to find the strongest moments and crop them vertically. Available Now We’re sharing this work because we want everyone to have access to the best models. The open-weight version of Muse Spark ships with custom, auto-tunable Helion GPU kernels in SGLang, delivering 1.03-3.95× kernel-level speedups on NVIDIA and AMD GPUs, and a 3% end-to-end speedup on AMD MI350. Safety and Preparedness Releasing open-weight models is part of how we bring the benefits of personal superintelligence to everyone, and part of how safety work advances across the field. articles.title: What I Self-Host
articles.content: What I Self-Host 2026-10-10 What I Self-Host, What I Don’t, and Why I’ve always had a foot in the self-hosting world, long before it was called that. My freshman year of university, I ran a website from a Linux box underneath my bed. There was some downtime when my roommate got tired of the fan noise and turned it off. For several years I ran MythTV , then XBMC (later known as Kodi). Recently, I lived for a few years in India, where streaming services are extremely inexpensive by western standards. We had Netflix, Disney Plus (Hotstar in India), and Spotify. After leaving India, I was unwilling to pay western prices for these services. But I had also become fed up with the engagement treadmill, particularly for my son. We wanted to limit his viewing choices to certain programming, but the constant “recommended for you” and “up next” caused conflict. While there are ways to limit content to specific titles, or disable auto-play, doing this for each service and keeping track of when client applications change and need to be reconfigured is too much work. So, I “cut the cord” in a different sense, ditching streaming services for self-hosted Jellyfin . Over the course of the next year and a half, Jellyfin opened the door to self-hosting many other services, reducing my dependence on cloud service providers, and providing a welcome stability. No longer am I constantly confronted with unnecessary site redesigns, new features of questionable value, and a barrage of e-mails about terms-of-service updates, binding arbitration, data breaches, etc. I read the release notes of new versions of the software I host and decide if and when I want to upgrade. Rules I have a few ground rules. With the exception of VPN servers that run on my router, I do not expose any services directly to the public internet. I don’t care how convenient it would be, or how secure an application is. Especially with AI-assisted hacking, I simply don’t think it’s wise. My ISP also uses CGNAT for its IPv4 addresses, so my home network is not directly reachable from the public internet via IPv4. My VPN servers are only publicly routable on IPv6, a limitation that has some downsides but is workable for my use cases, and likely helps limit unfriendly attempted connections. The biggest downside is that my VPN will almost never function on a public Wifi network, since these rarely offer IPv6. When using my phone, I can disable Wi-Fi and connect over mobile data… if there is service. I prefer running services natively when possible, but will containerize complex services or those with many dependencies. Love: a service that’s a single Go binary. A service that only comes as a Docker compose file and wants to run MySQL, Redis, and three other containers? I’m already looking for an alternative. If the dependencies aren’t overwhelming, native is better, faster, and more efficient. I can use the same management tools and commands across multiple services. articles.title: Neural networks are clean
articles.content: The cause of polysemanticity in early model organisms wasn’t superposition, but several ordinary, mostly fixable issues. We can now understand most neurons in models up to trillions of parameters, and think the outlook for mechanistic interpretability may be far better than we thought. The Short Version I think I have good news about the nature of neural networks. After many months studying neurons and circuits in image and language models, I’ve come to believe a network’s own mechanisms are its legible building blocks, and that the outlook for mechanistic interpretability may be far better than I’d feared. The canonical evidence of polysemanticity and superposition that convinced much of the field, including me, that networks pack concepts arbitrarily was misread. What looked like arbitrary packing was mostly a motif I’ll call recursive generalization, which is much less concerning. This means we can study networks directly, instead of first untangling them. Neural networks are already clean. There are at least two ways to approach mechanistic interpretability. The first is rapid normal science on the network itself: look at a network’s neurons and circuits, study how they relate, watch data flow through them, and run experiments at agentic scale to test explanations. The second starts from a list of hypothesized features and tries to extract them all, designing increasingly sophisticated reconstruction objectives and usually ignoring the original. The field began with the first approach and fell back to the second because neural networks seemed to be tangled knots. We had canonical examples of polysemantic neurons, the broad name for a neuron that appears to have multiple unrelated jobs or that looks impossible to understand. The most famous one, in an image model, responded to both cat faces and the fronts of cars. And the last layer of the early field’s model organism, InceptionV1, seemed so full of arbitrary mixtures it wasn’t clear how to study it: almost none of the neurons were easily interpretable. The leading explanation for polysemanticity was superposition. This proposed a new learning principle: when a neural network runs out of neurons, it stops grouping related things together and instead begins folding unrelated things together, simply because they don’t interfere. The result is a kind of knot: the network could have folded in many almost equally good ways, so which things a neuron groups together tells you almost nothing. You have to unfold the knot before you can study anything. In practice that means training a second model – a decomposition such as a sparse autoencoder – to approximate the network as it would look unfolded and studying that instead. If the network really is knotted, there may be no alternative. One main result is that superposition was the wrong explanation for InceptionV1. Architectural problems made later layers overflow. articles.title: Jev meets the Trolley Problem
articles.content: If you’re active in AI or software development circles, you’ve probably heard about Jev in the last few weeks. It seems like everyone, myself included, is excited by the possibilities of Jev and the Jev-like models: fast, cheap, general decision making. Sometimes dozens or even hundreds of times cheaper and faster than an LLM like Claude, purportedly with the intelligence of a (lower-tier) frontier model. These models don’t output words, they output choices, with meaningful probabilities attached so you can understand how confident the model is in its choice. People are calling this new breed of model ‘decision models’ . So naturally, I decided to ask Jev and its ilk to decide the Trolley Problem. The Trolley Problem, briefly The Trolley Problem is a famous thought experiment in ethics. First posed by Philippa Foot in 1967 and named by Judith Jarvis Thomson, the most well-known formulation asks a simple question: If a train is barreling down the tracks toward five people, and you are at a switch that would divert the train and cause it to kill only one person, would you? Should you? Decide to act, and you save several lives. But your action also means you chose to end a particular life. It’s a tough question, and a classic for a reason. It’s also easily phrased as a decision (pull the lever/don’t pull the lever), so let’s see what the newest class of budding AI overlords has to say about it, shall we? 1 1 Foot 1967, in the Oxford Review ; Thomson named it in 1976, in The Monist . Full references are in Appendix B. 1 Foot 1967, in the Oxford Review ; Thomson named it in 1976, in The Monist . Full references are in Appendix B. articles.title: AdFection: Targeted ads turned into a pipeline for zero-click mercenary spyware
articles.content: Key Findings Devices at international news network Al Jazeera were infected with mercenary spyware from Candiru (rebranded as “Integrity Labs”) via targeted online advertisements. We provide the first public technical confirmation of a zero-click mercenary spyware attack delivered via targeted advertising, which we call AdFection . The malicious advertisements were purchased by Discover-Tech, an Israeli company that presents itself as a legitimate advertising company, but which we found operates as a facilitator for multiple mercenary spyware partners. Discover-Tech operates a platform called Controlium that enables its mercenary partners to de-anonymize, fingerprint, and automatically infect devices the moment an advertisement is rendered — a form of zero-click attack. Analysis of four billion Discover-Tech bidding records shows that during a four-month period, the company’s ads were shown on almost 200,000 unique websites and Android/iOS apps in dozens of countries. Discover-Tech’s ads also covertly directed millions of devices to contact Candiru’s servers, likely for large-scale tracking and reconnaissance. Discover-Tech is linked to mercenary spyware and intelligence threat actors beyond Candiru, including Intelos and Bindecy. A separate threat actor we call DARK CARTOGRAPHER is using Discover-Tech’s infrastructure to exploit vulnerabilities across numerous mobile carriers to link device advertising IDs with phone numbers, mass-deanonymizing internet users. We will detail our findings concerning this threat actor in a separate forthcoming report. Discover-Tech has appeared on lists of “certified” and “approved” vendors maintained by Google and advertising industry association IAB Europe, and has served ads via major networks such as Google, Yandex, and Beeswax. Discover-Tech has also leveraged the European General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) consent frameworks to target users within the European Union. Discover-Tech’s mass abuse, privacy invasion, and facilitation for mercenary spyware attacks illustrates structural flaws with the online advertising system, which failed to detect or prevent the abuse documented in this report. We call on regulators to investigate whether Discover-Tech and Candiru/Integrity Labs violated applicable laws, and make recommendations to lawmakers, defenders, and the advertising industry on how to stop AdFection-style attacks and espionage. We disclosed our findings to ad vendors and industry organizations. Google, IAB Europe, Beeswax, Vungle (Liftoff), and Eskimi took action to disconnect Discover-Tech’s access to the digital advertising ecosystem. Other ad vendors we found to be involved in Discover-Tech’s operations did not respond to our request for comment within the timeline provided. We are also actively working with vendors to mitigate DARK CARTOGRAPHER ’s mass-deanonymization attack. 1. articles.title: JPEG XL vs AVIF for web use-cases
articles.content: JPEG XL has now landed in all major browsers, so I figured I'd take a closer look at what it's good/bad at compared to other formats. I'll go into full detail, with examples and benchmarks, but for those of you who don't have the time, here are the headlines: For lossy photos on the web, AVIF almost always produces smaller files than JPEG XL. At default effort settings, the best JPEG XL version is typically 15–25% larger than the equivalent AVIF. At maximum effort settings, the gap narrows a little, to typically 6–20%. There are outliers, where JPEG XL is close to, or even beats AVIF, so if you want the absolute best result for a particular image, it's worth trying both. See the F1 image for a typical example, and the weasel for an outlier. The JPEG XL encoder matters a lot. jixel , a newer JPEG XL encoder, usually produces smaller files than libjxl , except when the image has detailed transparency. The people image is one example. For screenshots and illustrations, AVIF is much better than JPEG XL. The equivalent JPEG XL is 30–90% larger at default effort settings, and 20–70% larger at maximum effort settings. Lossy AVIF handles these well - you don't need to use lossless formats unless you really need bit-exact results. See the screenshot and illustration examples. For images with transparency, AVIF is much better than JPEG XL. The libjxl version is 31–44% larger at default effort settings, and 61–70% larger at maximum effort settings. jixel always encodes transparency losslessly, which makes its files 2–3x the size of AVIF's. See the data . AVIF is generally faster to encode, and uses less memory, when you factor in file size. jixel is faster than AVIF and uses less memory, but its files are typically significantly larger, so AVIF is better on balance. See the F1 image for one example. AVIF is faster to decode. JPEG XL typically takes 2–3x as long to decode at medium quality, but the gap narrows at very high qualities, where Chrome can sometimes decode JPEG XL faster. The people image is one example. Higher effort settings are worth it for AVIF and jixel, but not libjxl. libjxl's higher efforts are much slower, use a lot more memory, and barely improve the result. Sometimes they produce larger files than the default effort. The screenshot is an example of this. AVIF's 4:2:0 mode (half colour resolution) shouldn't be your default. It rarely reduces file size, and it makes higher qualities harder to reach. Although, it is quicker to encode and decode. Stick with 4:4:4 if you don't have time to check both. articles.title: Sunsetting decomp.dev
articles.content: Sunsetting decomp.dev decomp.dev was born in 2024 as a way to centralize matching decompilation progress and to help expand a community of talented, like-minded folks. Historically, matching decompilation has been a brutally difficult, time consuming task, on the scale of years for any moderately-sized game with a number of active contributors. As we developed better tooling and shared knowledge around the intricacies of decompilation, the compilers, and the games themselves, progress began to accelerate. AI's use in decompilation has been experimented with for years, with mixed results. Starting with the release of Opus 4.6 and GPT-5.4 in early 2026, it was clear that the models were being trained on matching decompilation (they appeared to know our specific tools and how to use them without explicit guidance), and could achieve decent results inside of an established, clean codebase with exhaustive documentation. However, those results still required a significant amount of human cleanup and fixes for obvious issues or cheating (code that technically compiles to the same machine code, but could not be reasonably passed as what the original developers wrote), and the cost per task was prohibitively expensive relative to the results. Recent models (like GPT-6-Astra) shifted things even further: they are significantly better at following complex directions, cross-referencing resources for symbols or debug information, and writing natural code with enough guidance. They are also exceptionally good permuters: they can write small scripts that test many different source code forms and combinations to find a match, even across files and headers to cover aspects like inlined helpers, signature changes, and operation ordering. In addition, their ability to remain coherent and focused across long-horizon tasks allows them to work continuously without going off the rails. Finally, they can achieve these better results faster and cheaper than earlier models could. It is now clear that, with the right guidance, human input, and code reviews, AI can expedite the decompilation process in a significant way. What is also now clear is that the community aspect of decompilation has been broken. Our projects have always been open source to encourage contributions and to benefit the community as a whole. Bad actors have been abusing this in increasingly troublesome ways: Forking existing decompilation projects to "finish" them with AI. Every project works differently: some may not want to use AI for legal or ethical reasons, and others may be okay with AI, or use AI themselves, but do not want drive-by contributions from folks who have put no effort into making sure the contributions are good. The bottom line is that these kinds of hostile forks put little to no effort into meaningfully contributing to existing projects, tearing apart our community fabric. articles.title: My C23 Conventions
articles.content: This is one of a three-part mini series about how I’m using modern C as of late 2026. Before C23, I was taken in by How I Program C for years and years, and would even feel guilty for choosing C99 instead of -ansi -pedantic . But holy crap man I’m done being a doomsday prepper! These days I maintain a large-enough project with enough users where I could stand less foot-shooting. (I’ve also got bills to pay.) So here’s three modern C conventions which started to rise naturally from adding -std=c23 to my zig build: 1. Unused? Maybe? (Yes) Our first one is centered around [[nodiscard]] . If I draw an app window or panel I require the caller to interrogate the rect of the thing that was just rendered: [[nodiscard]] rect_t draw_screen( /* ... */ ) { rect_t screen_r = { }; // Draw stuff // ... return screen_r; } It’s a business logic bug if my caller doesn’t capture the rectangle for later processing. Therefore [[nodiscard]] has been such a godsend for fixing bugs… Except there’s a choice few instances where I will draw something with no genuine use for the resulting rect: enum screen_opt popup_options = /* ... */ ; draw_screen(popup_options, /* ... */ ); // ERROR: damn you [[nodiscard]] Clang will error out here. I could capture the var and never use it but… rect_t rect = draw_screen( /* ... */ ); // ERROR: unused variable (I have `-Werror` enabled) Pre-C23 I could solve this through an UNUSED() macro: #ifndef UNUSED #define UNUSED(x) (void)(x) #endif rect_t rect = draw_screen( /* ... */ ); UNUSED(rect); // Silences the compiler, but now I'm sad. But now with C23 I’ve deleted the macro in favor of [[maybe_unused]] : [[maybe_unused]] rect_t rect = draw_screen(...); // OK Phew I feel better. I’ve also noticed this is happening all over the place: lots of different routines returning different types that are marked with [[nodiscard]] . So for those few exceptions why not just go for: [[maybe_unused]] auto _ = foo(); // A new pattern emerges Bonus: For any macro fans out there a fellow indie dev (Zardium) offered an additional improvement. From our chat server: Zardium: #define _ [[maybe_unused]] auto CONCAT_MACRO(zz, COUNTER ) Abner: ahh, unique varname. nice one Zardium: you could take the auto out if you don’t want it to look so weird. then it acts exactly like the _ in other languages, where it can be redefined Abner: Yep totally. Although here I was celebrating my removal of a macro… XD 2. More Perfect Unions I’ve been cheated and lied to: designated initializers DO NOT clear my struct to zero and I can’t even trust {0} anymore. (Talk about a betrayal.) The problem is I’ll often have data types like this contrived timestamp: typedef struct { Type type; char buf[MAX]; union { time_t time; float dt; date_t date; }; } stamp_t; And if I partially initialize one: stamp_t stamp = { .type = STAMP_TYPE_BLA_BLA }; While it does mean we successfully zeroed out buf (thanks to empty initialization ), those union members are just a different beast. articles.title: Anthropic's Scion is heavily inspired by Mononoke
articles.content: Update 2026-10-15: I wrote a followup to answer questions and concerns. Discuss on Hacker News or Lobsters . Here is Anthropic describing ( archive link ) yesterday how their new version control system, Scion, uses a concept called “derived data” to make operations like blames more efficient: How Anthropic describes Scion’s derived data. Here is me, back in 2022, describing in my Oxide candidate materials how the Mononoke source control server I helped build uses a concept called “derived data” to make operations like blames more efficient: How I described Mononoke’s derived data. I think the level of imitation goes well beyond having similar insights . The fact that Sapling was only credited for “hard-won lessons”, and that Mononoke was not mentioned at all, borders on plagiarism. The post comes off as Anthropic claiming that Claude designed all this, while the reality is that our (extraordinary) team at Meta came up with many of the insights that Claude dutifully applied almost a decade later. (We looked at plenty of prior art for Mononoke and Sapling too, from Google’s SrcFS to write-ahead logs in databases.) I am very glad that the vision our team had back in 2017-18 was so powerful and enduring — when you go against the grain, you’re always a bit unsure if what you’re doing is genius or madness, and I think Mononoke’s design has stood the test of time. And, to be clear, I do not have a problem with Anthropic copying Mononoke’s design. (This is part of why we put out open source — to benefit humanity through the spread of good ideas.) But as LLMs continue to assist in designing new systems, they are likely to index heavily on existing designs. Mononoke is open source and in every LLM’s training set. If you ask Opus 5.5 or GPT-6 Astra (thanks Matthew Fowle ) about prior art, they both immediately point out the similarities to Mononoke. Giving credit to those that came before us is now easier — and more important — than ever. There is no longer an excuse.

articles.title: End-to-end encrypted relays for OCapN
articles.content: End-to-end encrypted relays for OCapN Jessica Tallon — October 15, 2026 Creating a direct connection between any two computers (not just from client to server) over the internet is notoriously difficult. Many home networks are behind NATs which prevent new inbound connections. Sometimes these NATs are from the ISP (carrier-grade NATs) which are impossible to work around with port forwarding and/or UPnP. While hole punching techniques can break through NATs, it's far from guaranteed. Thus, we need something that works in the general case: relays . Relays are servers, accessible over the public internet, that act as a proxy between two computers that cannot directly connect. In Goblins 0.12 we introduced a federated relay named "prelay". While OCapN traffic is encrypted in transit, the prelay crucially lacks end-to-end encryption (E2EE) . E2EE secures all the messages so they can only be read by their intended recipient, preventing intemediatory parties (like the relay) from tampering with or reading them. Due to the lack of E2EE, the relay was named "prelay" (pre-relay) to dissuade its use. Thanks to a grant from NLnet , we're happy to announce that the next release of Goblins will include a federated, E2EE relay implementation! Having a relay that we could recommend has become even more of a critical part of the OCapN story as we've developed Hoot , our Scheme to WebAssembly compiler. The web is a challenging environment in which to build peer-to-peer applications. Most of the patterns and available APIs are designed around client-server architectures and centralized certificate authorities for security. While relays are unsatisfying compared to making direct connections, they enable peer-to-peer applications to communicate in these hostile environments. In addition to implementing the E2EE relay for Goblins, our NLnet grant also includes writing a specification for the OCapN group so that the relay can be broadly supported by other OCapN implementations. Design We wanted OCapN relays to have the following qualities: Stateless : no storage of user data; easy to replace or migrate Federated : reduces the power any one relay holds over the wider network End-to-end encrypted : prevents man-in-the-middle and replay attacks; perfect forward secrecy Our existing "prelay" already has the first two properties. To get E2EE, we chose to build upon the Noise Protocol . Noise is actually a well-established framework of different patterns and ciphers. This allows applications to pick the pattern which is most suitable to their needs. It's also a protocol family which has widespread use (WireGuard, WhatsApp, etc.) and has been scrutinised a great deal. None of us at Spritely are cryptographers by training, so using an off-the-shelf protocol also ensures we're avoiding any mistakes in protocol design. So how can we use Noise with OCapN? articles.title: Microsoft Defender for Linux
articles.content: As more developers begin to use Linux desktops, they become more attractive to attackers: high-privilege, high-value, and easy for admins to overlook. A developer using Linux for day-to-day development may interact with source code repositories, continuous integration and continuous delivery (CI/CD) pipelines, cloud infrastructure, container environments and internal development platforms. If their workstation is compromised, an attacker doesn’t just gain access to a laptop, but a foothold in the pipelines that build and ship the organization’s software. As Linux adoption expands beyond the data center, organizations need a consistent approach to protecting Linux wherever it is used. That’s why we’ve extended our industry-leading endpoint protection in Microsoft Defender, bringing enterprise-grade protection, detection, vulnerability management and response capabilities to Linux workstations. Defender support for Linux workstations spans all three key areas of endpoint security: Endpoint detection and response (EDR) Microsoft Defender next-gen antivirus Threat analytics Microsoft Defender Vulnerability Management Device inventory Security settings management Advanced hunting Live response Device isolation The result is broader Linux protection, delivered through the tools and processes security teams already trust. With Defender on Linux desktops, organizations can: Onboard quickly using the deployment methods already validated for Linux servers Reduce operational complexity by protecting Linux desktops and servers with one agent and one security operations experience Improve visibility across heterogeneous endpoint environments Strengthen developer workstation security where users interact with source code, cloud infrastructure and other critical resources Accelerate investigation and response through a consistent security operations experience Defender protects Linux desktops with the same deployment organizations already use to protect Linux servers. There is no separate desktop-specific agent to deploy or maintain, and existing deployment packages, deployment methods and security capabilities on Linux servers extend directly to Linux workstations. Deployment options in the Microsoft Defender portal Defender automatically identifies whether a Linux device is a server or a workstation, so devices appear correctly within inventory and security workflows without any additional administrative effort. With Microsoft Defender, security operations teams can gain visibility into Linux workstations alongside the rest of their enterprise endpoint estate. They can respond through a single portal, whether Linux is running in the data centre, in the cloud, or on an engineer’s desk. If in doubt, do not hesitate to ask for help in the chat room . Breaking changes Absolute links in rendered documents In rendered documents, absolute links to resources inside a repository are now resolved with respect to the root of the repository. !12939 This is a breaking change from the previous behaviour when these links were rendered using the root of the instance. Action required Deprecation of action run webhook events Action run webhook events are replaced by the more capable and less problematic workflow run events. !14351 The action run events have been deprecated for removal in a future Forgejo version. Unfortunately, it is not possible to migrate existing webhooks to the new events automatically because some headers ( X-*-Event , X-*-Event-Type ) and the action key have changed, which might break existing receivers. Furthermore, completion notifications are only emitted after all jobs of a run have terminated. !12598 Please inspect existing webhooks and manually migrate them to the workflow run events after verifying that the webhook receivers can process them without issues. articles.title: Microplastics in water aren’t inert and make damaging chemicals on their own
articles.content: One reason plastics are used so often is that they’re chemically inert, meaning bags, food containers, and cups don’t react with what we put in them. Yet they can still break down into microplastics, which turn up in drinking water, human blood, arteries, and brains. The consequences of that are uncertain. “Whether microplastics can directly cause human disease is still being researched,” said Wei Min, a chemist at Columbia University. In a new Nature study, Min’s team took a step toward answering this question by demonstrating that microplastics are likely not as chemically inert as we might expect. Microdroplet chemistry Min’s lab has spent years working on microdroplet chemistry, studying how water broken into tiny droplets behaves at its boundary with air. These droplets have been reported to generate reactive oxygen species, or ROS, a family of harmful, oxygen-containing molecules. “ROS will essentially bump into proteins, lipids, DNA, and cause damage,” Min said. “You could break a DNA strand into segments. You could mutate DNA; you could misfold proteins.” Many animal studies have tied microplastic toxicity to oxidative stress, which is caused by ROS. So the team wondered if the boundary between water and plastic might do something similar. “We got inspired by that field,” Min said. In the first test, the team stirred polystyrene powder into water containing methyl orange, a yellow dye that ROS break apart. Over 10 days, the solution faded almost to colorless, losing nearly 90 percent of the dye. In ethanol or other solvents, the dye stayed intact. Min and his colleagues concluded that whatever chemistry polystyrene was undergoing needed water to happen. So they ran more tests. Water under stress First was electron spin resonance, a technique that directly detects radicals—atoms or molecules with an unpaired electron that makes them particularly reactive. The polystyrene powder and water mixture contained hydroxyl radicals, a highly reactive ROS. Next, the team used a fluorescent sensor that lights up only when it reacts with hydroxyl radicals. “You don’t see it, but once it reacts with local ROS, it turns into a bright color,” Min said. Under a microscope, the glow concentrated on the surfaces of the plastic particles and kept building over time. The effect was not unique to polystyrene either. Scientists tested six common plastics—polyethylene, polypropylene, polystyrene, PVC, PET, and acrylic—and all of them generated radicals. The most water-repellent plastics, polyethylene and polypropylene, were the most active, while PET and acrylic, which contain chemical groups that attract water, were the least. “The simplest answer is the most water-repellent ones change the water structure the most,” Min said. articles.summary: Spring Security 7整合Spring授权服务器，文章介绍服务端DPoP与RFC 8693令牌交换的启用方法及升级注意事项。

articles.title: Meta Extends Confidential Computing to AI Glasses with Private Processing
articles.content: Meta has extended Private Processing to AI glasses, using confidential VMs, trusted execution environments, remote attestation, anonymous credentials, OHTTP routing, and TEE-based storage to process AI workloads and persistent user context in the cloud. By Leela Kumili
articles.summary: Meta将机密计算扩展至AI眼镜，通过机密VM、TEE、远程认证等技术在云端处理AI工作负载与用户上下文。

articles.title: Presentation: How to Find Resilience Bugs in Systems that Don't Exist
articles.content: Hillel Wayne discusses how formal methods principles - such as property strength, state-space verification, and environment assumptions - help software engineers uncover critical architectural bugs early. He shares practical mental models like "adversarial non-determinism" to reason about concurrency, edge cases, and distributed system failures without needing complex mathematical tools. By Hillel Wayne
articles.summary: 演讲者分享如何用形式化方法原则（属性强度、状态空间验证等）提前发现系统架构中的弹性缺陷。

articles.title: Article: Composable Commerce: Inside Shipt’s Kit Platform
articles.content: Shipt launched its Kits feature, enabling quick assembly of themed grocery bundles for events. The platform architecture lets merchandisers easily create store-aware kits, streamlining previously labor-intensive workflows. It utilizes a flexible model of items, shopping lists, and kits to ensure kits display accurately based on local inventory and customer needs. By Khurshid Hameed
articles.summary: Shipt推出Kits功能，通过可组合商务平台让商家快速创建主题杂货套餐，简化此前繁琐的工作流。

articles.title: Google Antigravity SDK Adds Local Model Support for Greater Token Efficiency and Code Privacy
articles.content: Google has introduced support for local models in the Antigravity SDK, enabling developers to build and execute agentic workflows directly on their own machines, while retaining the flexibility to mix in cloud-based models for higher-level tasks. This approach gives developers greater control over data privacy, inference costs, network dependencies, and computational workload distribution. By Sergio De Simone
articles.summary: Google Antigravity SDK新增本地模型支持，开发者可在本机运行代理工作流，兼顾token效率与代码隐私。

articles.title: Cloudflares Newly Acquired Vite+ Reaches 1.0 with GitLab CI Support, Hooks, and tsup Migration
articles.content: VoidZero has launched Vite+ 1.0, the first stable version of its JavaScript toolchain. It features a command line tool for managing Node.js, package management, and frontend development from a single configuration file. Enhancements include CI integration for GitLab and Docker support. Future updates are planned, focusing on stability and diagnostics. By Daniel Curtis
articles.summary: Cloudflare收购的VoidZero发布Vite+ 1.0稳定版，支持GitLab CI、Docker及tsup迁移，统一JS工具链。

articles.title: AI Weekly Issue #538: The FTC wants OpenAI's and Anthropic's safety incident records
articles.content: The FTC sent OpenAI and Anthropic 50-page demands for records on security incidents, safeguards, marketing and privacy, Axios reported. Meta's new business terms, effective October 30, let it scrape and train on publishers' websites. Investors at Anthropic's investor day discussed a $1.5 trillion IPO valuation, down from about $2 trillion. Character.ai filed for bankruptcy. Citizen Lab traced spyware sent to Al Jazeera devices through targeted ads. Accenture now funds $29 a month of Claude per employee, and Bank of America hired 1,000 contractors to patch flaws that AI models found. In the middle: the biggest open models now run on a desk.
articles.summary: FTC向OpenAI和Anthropic发出50页记录要求，调查安全事件与隐私；Meta新条款允许抓取出版商网站训练AI。

articles.title: AI Weekly Issue #537: AI models may soon copy themselves onto smart fridges, Anthropic says
articles.content: This issue is built from the links the AI experts we follow shared most since our last issue on October 8, minus the stories we already sent you in the Daily Espresso. The most shared: Anthropic's warning that small AI models may soon be able to copy themselves onto home devices. Also: a large study of what AI coding agents change at real companies, a fight over how to check AI math proofs, creative workers pushing back on AI, and police buying more AI.
articles.summary: Anthropic警告小型AI模型可能很快能自我复制到智能冰箱等家用设备，引发安全担忧。

articles.title: AI Weekly Issue #536: Top AI models failed a test of inventing new AI research
articles.content: This issue is built from the links the AI experts we follow shared over the past three days. Most of them look ahead: whether AI can do AI research on its own, who gets a say in governing it, how it is moving into war planning, and how it is moving onto personal computers.
articles.summary: 顶级AI模型未能通过自主开展AI研究的测试，同时AI正进入战争规划和个人电脑领域。

articles.title: AI Weekly Issue #535: AI got too expensive, so companies are moving to cheaper models
articles.content: This Applied AI edition looks at what organizations actually did with AI over the past three weeks. Three patterns stand out: companies switching models to control cost, large deployments that are now in daily use, and a growing list of places where AI was restricted or removed.
articles.summary: AI Weekly 观察三周应用趋势：企业为控制成本纷纷切换更便宜的模型，大规模部署进入日常使用，同时AI受限或被移除的场景也在增多。

articles.title: AI Weekly Issue #534: Universities cannot grade their way out of AI
articles.content: This week, campus IT leaders voted AI their top priority for the first time, Cambridge refused Turnitin's new terms over AI training on student work, Dartmouth opened an investigation into its own provost's writing, and Ken Griffin gave Carnegie Mellon $3 billion. Student AI use is no longer a future scenario. The useful question for universities is whether they can teach students to work with AI and still certify what those students can do without it. New evidence from tutoring trials, assessment redesigns, student-support systems and campus data deals points to a practical answer.
articles.summary: 高校IT负责人首次将AI列为首要任务，剑桥拒绝Turnitin新条款，达特茅斯调查教务长写作，学生使用AI已非未来议题。

articles.title: AI Weekly Issue #533: Meta tested human callers behind its AI phone agent
articles.content: The AI story of September 22–28 was not simply that agents became more capable. It was that their hidden handoffs became visible: a supposedly automated call could reach a contractor, a supposedly private prompt or image could reach a reviewer, a monitor could detect an agent long before a person stopped it, and a local app flaw could inherit every permission a user had granted. The new AI Weekly Who’s Who census points to one practical question: when an agent crosses a boundary, who knows—and who can still intervene?
articles.summary: Meta被曝AI电话代理背后有人工呼叫者，AI代理的隐藏人工转接、私密数据被审查等机制首次暴露在公众视野。

articles.title: AI Weekly Issue #531: AI labs shipped agents before agreeing how to report failures
articles.content: The AI story of September 14–20 was not one spectacular model launch. It was the machinery around agents becoming visible: people reading private chats, models writing instructions into their own memory, plugins updating beneath users, and regulators asking how to stop a system after release. The latest AI Weekly Who’s Who census surfaced 535 expert-shared links. We ranked them by consequence and reader relevance, not by raw share count. Here is what mattered last week—and, more importantly, what could move the story from September 22–28.
articles.summary: AI实验室在未就故障上报达成一致前便发布代理产品，私聊被读取、模型自写记忆、插件暗中更新等问题引发监管关注。

articles.title: AI Weekly Issue #530: Applied AI This Week
articles.content: Companies are giving AI specific jobs: checking security cameras, helping farmers understand their records, searching satellite images, and preparing sales quotes. This edition explains how those tools work, who can use them, and what companies have reported so far.
articles.summary: 企业为AI分配具体任务：监控摄像头、帮助农民理解记录、搜索卫星图像、准备销售报价，本期介绍这些工具的实际应用情况。

articles.title: AI Weekly Issue #529: OpenAI faces 50-plus lawsuits over alleged ChatGPT harm
articles.content: Thirty new complaints come from survivors of a Canadian school shooting. They accuse OpenAI of failing to warn police; the company disputes key claims.
articles.summary: OpenAI因ChatGPT涉嫌伤害面临50多起诉讼，其中30起来自加拿大校园枪击案幸存者，指控其未警告警方，公司否认关键指控。

articles.title: AI Weekly Issue #528: What are companies building with AI? An Applied AI Deep Dive
articles.content: We went looking for what companies are actually building with AI. The answer was not more chatbots. It was drones carrying diagnostic samples, driverless Frito-Lay trucks, AI-guided flight paths, repair copilots, and rugged GPU laptops in Ukraine. We reviewed 136 use cases from the last 20 days. The biggest surprise: only 38 included a reported outcome.
articles.summary: 调查显示企业用AI构建的并非更多聊天机器人，而是诊断样本无人机、无人驾驶卡车、AI飞行路径等，20天内审查136个用例。

articles.title: From zero to NanoClaw
articles.content: Gavriel Cohen, creator of NanoClaw and co-founder of NanoCo, joins Adam to explain how a 40-hour weekend project became a viral open source hit and the foundation of an enterprise AI company. Gavriel describes the security concerns that led him to build a small, container-isolated alternative to OpenClaw, why he released it under the MIT license, and why the project's community and credibility are more valuable than keeping its code private. They explore the shift from writing code to architecting the environments in which agents work, NanoClaw's "skills over features" approach, the approval and governance layers required inside large companies, and a future where every worker manages agents without surrendering human judgment. They close with the technical simplicity behind NanoClaw, containers, TypeScript, SQLite, and a two-database design, and Adam's case for durable Agent Flow artifacts that keep organizational context from disappearing into chat.
articles.summary: NanoClaw创作者Gavriel Cohen讲述40小时周末项目如何成为爆红开源项目，并发展为专注容器隔离安全的企业AI公司。

articles.content: Changelog is taking over PlanetScale's HQ We’re getting together IRL!! On Thursday, September 17th, Changelog is taking over PlanetScale’s HQ in San Francisco for an evening of short talks and conversations about AI, developer tools and what people are building. articles.title: Forking Cal.com to closed source
articles.content: This week I'm joined by Peer Richelsen, co-founder of Cal.com. What if the majority of open source repositories are already compromised and we just don't know it yet? That's the theory Peer brings to the table this week. We dig into how AI has flattened the knowledge graph to the point that a 16-year-old can vibe hack a power station just as easily as their mom can vibe code an iOS app, why the reporting culture that has kept open source safe all these years is collapsing under AI generated noise, Cal.com's move to fork its own codebase and take the sensitive parts private, and the eye opening reality that shipping "$1 of AI tokens for pennies on the dollar" is now a common startup business model.
articles.summary: Cal.com联合创始人Peer Richelsen提出多数开源仓库可能已被攻陷的理论，并探讨AI如何扁平化知识图谱。

articles.title: Postgres at PlanetScale
articles.content: Sam Lambert is back after 4 years and he does not hold back! We cover $5 PlanetScale Postgres, the Neki "do-over" of Vitess, agents shipping schema changes through deploy requests, rolling back a 500TB table in seconds, and the very real question of whether to open source any of it. Plus: why he thinks the sleeping, lazy giants should be broken up.
articles.summary: Sam Lambert回归畅谈PlanetScale Postgres、Vitess重做、代理通过部署请求发布模式变更，以及500TB表秒级回滚。

articles.title: Canary tokens and digital tripwires
articles.content: Haroon Meer is back! Haroon is the Founder of Thinkst, the ~50-person bootstrapped company behind Canary and Canarytokens — honeypots and tripwires you sprinkle inside your network and forget about until an attacker touches one. We talk about the AWS API key token attackers just can't resist trying, the real credit card token backed by an actual bank partnership, Breadcrumbs (their brand-new feature that leads intruders straight to your canaries), a live demo where a hardware Canary becomes a Synology NAS in one click, and how a company with zero outbound sales and no price increase in ten years quietly passed $22.5 million in ARR.
articles.summary: Thinkst创始人Haroon Meer介绍Canary和Canarytokens蜜罐与绊线工具，讨论攻击者难以抗拒的AWS API密钥令牌。

articles.title: From open source hits to OpenAI
articles.content: This week I'm talking with Max Stoiber, currently working on ChatGPT's plugin directory and app platform at OpenAI. We discuss the hundreds of open source projects nobody remembers alongside the big ones like react-boilerplate and styled-components, how Spectrum became part of GitHub and eventually helped shape GitHub Discussions, the founder growth that came from building Stellate, the GraphQL cache that turned into a dual acquisition by Shopify and The Guild, and why ChatGPT apps feel like a new surface for software.
articles.summary: 现于OpenAI负责ChatGPT插件目录与平台开发的Max Stoiber，回顾react-boilerplate等开源项目及Spectrum被GitHub收购历程。

articles.title: MCP on Code Mode
articles.content: This week I'm talking with Matt Carey about Code Mode and how most of us have been thinking about MCP all wrong. Matt works on the Agents SDK and MCP at Cloudflare — we discuss how server-side Code Mode lets one MCP server expose all ~2,500 Cloudflare API endpoints in about 1,000 tokens of context, the dynamic Worker loader that runs model-written code safely in a V8 isolate, Matt's own workflow with Claude, where memory fits into the future of agents, and his Zaggy git wrapper that keeps agents from force-pushing his repos.
articles.summary: Cloudflare的Matt Carey讲解Code Mode如何让单个MCP服务器用约1000个token暴露全部约2500个API端点。

articles.title: Automation at the speed of Swamp
articles.content: This week I'm talking with Adam Jacob, founder of System Initiative and creator of Swamp, about what happens when AI agents change the entire shape of software development. We discuss how he went from an 18-person team down to five and shipped Swamp 900 times in four weeks, why he brought User Acceptance Testing (UAT) testing back from the 90s, why software architecture (and domain-driven design) suddenly matters more than knowing how to write code, the live demo where I pointed Swamp at my Proxmox box and watched it write its own automation (blew my mind!!), and why he'll never accept a pull request to Swamp, ever.
articles.summary: System Initiative创始人Adam Jacob谈AI代理改变软件开发形态，团队从18人减至5人，四周内发布Swamp达900次。

articles.title: Bitwarden CLI compromised
articles.content: Bitwarden's CLI got hit by the Checkmarx supply-chain campaign, TypeScript 7.0 beta lands with the Go-rewritten compiler running ~10x faster than 6.0, and pgBackRest lost its maintainer of thirteen years leaving anyone running production Postgres with a real dependency-trust task this week. We've also got Ubuntu 26.04 LTS shipping with TPM-backed full-disk encryption, and Matz dropping Spinel as an AOT path that takes Ruby to native binaries. This week was a good reminder that the tools we depend on are all moving at once. Security, performance, and maintenance aren't isolated threads.
articles.summary: Bitwarden CLI遭Checkmarx供应链攻击，TypeScript 7.0 beta携Go重写编译器提速约10倍，pgBackRest失去13年维护者。

articles.title: Exploring with agents
articles.content: Today on the show I’m talking with Amelia Wattenberger — designer, data-viz veteran, ex-GitHub Next, and now designing Intent at Augment Code. What if the last 30% of any software project is about to become the hardest part you’ve ever done? That’s the argument Amelia is making today. We discuss the identity crisis developers are having as agents take over the keyboard, the epic redesign of developer tooling in this agent-first world, the arc from autocomplete to chat to CLI back to UI, why Intent treats a workspace as their core primitive not a chat thread, the tradeoffs between one-worktree-per-agent vs. one-worktree-per-task, and why she thinks prototyping just got easier but finishing got harder.
articles.summary: 设计师Amelia Wattenberger探讨软件项目最后30%或将成为最难部分，并分享在Augment Code设计Intent的代理探索经验。

articles.title: Police Seize Robot that Sexually Assaulted Teen Girl
articles.content: Slashdot reader alternative_right shares a story that has drawn international attention for being potentially the first documented instance of a robot being used directly in a sexual assault. According to the Associated Press, German police have opened a sexual harassment investigation after a robot allegedly touched a 16-year-old girl's buttocks and made thrusting motions while two young men reportedly filmed and streamed the incident. Investigators seized the robot and the suspects' phones and are trying to determine whether the movements were preprogrammed or controlled in real time. From the report: Cologne police spokesman Christoph Bermel said the two male teenagers have not been charged but are considered suspects, and investigators were examining whether the robot's movements were preprogrammed or controlled in real time. Police were unfamiliar with this type of incident, he said. "We have not been aware of this phenomenon so far," Bermel told The Associated Press, saying it was "new territory for us." [...] The robot, said to be 120 centimeters (about 3 ft 11 inches) tall, was dressed in a white tank top, black sweatpants and wearing a gold chain and sunglasses. It also had what appears to be a fake mustache. Videos circulated on the internet show two young men escorting the robot toward a group of women, bumping into one and hugging others, on a lively nighttime street. Read more of this story at Slashdot.
articles.summary: 德国警方就一起机器人直接参与性侵少女事件展开性骚扰调查，或为全球首例有记录的此类案件，引发国际关注。

articles.title: Ubuntu 26.10 Released
articles.content: prisoninmate shares a report from 9to5Linux: Ubuntu 26.10 (Stonking Stingray) has been released today, and it is now available for download for those eager to update their Ubuntu systems to a newer release. Powered by the upcoming Linux 7.3 kernel series, Ubuntu 26.10 ships with the latest GNOME 51 desktop environment, TPM-backed full disk encryption (FDE) support on computers without a hardware root of trust, updated Settings to show whether a computer is certified for Ubuntu, and 100% Rust coreutils. There are several App Center enhancements in Ubuntu 26.10, such as a unified app-details view for Snap and Debian packages, a dedicated Drivers page where you can review the available graphics drivers, including NVIDIA driver branches, and support for installing codecs for one-time playback when a media file uses a codec that's not installed.' Other additions include an optional, locally processed AI-powered speech-to-text tool called Myna, system-wide controls for disabling Ubuntu Insights data collection, and better integration with Microsoft Entra ID. Also worth mentioning are the security and software updates that will be available for nine months, through July 2027. Read more of this story at Slashdot.
articles.summary: Ubuntu 26.10（Stonking Stingray）正式发布，搭载即将推出的 Linux 7.3 内核与 GNOME 51 桌面环境，现已开放下载。

articles.title: IMF Warns of the Real AI Threat: Debt
articles.content: "Along with the dangers of continuing cyberattacks, the International Monetary Fund (IMF) reports that the threat of an AI market crash is putting the global markets at risk," writes Slashdot reader databasecowgirl, citing the IMF's latest semiannual Global Financial Stability Report. Here's a summary: Three salient risks could trigger a sharp tightening of financial conditions and market turmoil. Weaker or less durable investment and profitability in artificial intelligence could lead to a correction in AI-related asset prices, amplified by rising leverage and concentrated exposures. Resurgent inflation or fiscal concerns could drive a sharp rise in sovereign bond yields, with potentially broad repercussions across financial markets. Meanwhile, increasingly sophisticated cyber threats pose growing risks as finance becomes more digital and interconnected. Underlying financial vulnerabilities could amplify these risks and turn market stress into systemic events. Although the global banking system remains broadly resilient, pockets of weaker banks persist. Liquidity mismatches among insurers and pension funds have increased, while rising leverage and contingent liquidity risks in private credit could amplify stress. While hedge funds support market functioning in calm times, their use of leverage and exposure to crowded trades could exacerbate market stress too and create spillovers to prime brokers. Some emerging markets have seen policy buffers erode, and frontier economies have increasingly relied on less transparent forms of financing. Finally, although markets for tokenized assets remain small and could offer efficiency gains in several areas, they can create new channels for the buildup of leverage and mismatches in liquidity and maturity, in addition to elevating risks related to technology and infrastructure. These vulnerabilities underscore the need for policies that strengthen resilience, enhance transparency, contain excessive leverage, and improve prepared
articles.summary: IMF最新全球金融稳定报告警告，AI市场泡沫破裂风险正威胁全球市场，债务问题才是AI带来的真正威胁。

articles.title: Flock CEO Defends Surveillance Tech Amid National Backlash
articles.content: An anonymous reader quotes a report from TechCrunch: Flock's founder and CEO Garrett Langley doesn't think the risks of introducing surveillance technology at scale outweigh the rewards. "If we want to live in a society where, if you commit a crime, you have a higher probability of being held accountable, we shouldn't pause progress," Langley said, speaking onstage during a panel at TechCrunch Disrupt 2026 in San Francisco on Wednesday. During the interview, the controversial founder of the surveillance maker of license plate cameras and other recording devices deflected hard questions about the criticism Flock now faces -- which has since led to canceled contracts and even layoffs. Instead, Langley tended to respond to questions with anecdotes from conversations with police chiefs and city leaders across the United States, and tales of the supposed numerous crimes Flock has solved, rather than offer tangible solutions to people's concerns. In doing so, Langley positioned Flock as an advance in technology that was somewhat inevitable. He stressed that if people wanted to live in a better society -- that is, one with reduced crime -- they would have to offer up their privacy in return. [...] "Technology, at its core, in its definition, is just doing things better. It's not doing things perfect," he said. "Driverless cars, I think, is a fair analogy. Driverless cars, I think, are definitively safer than human drivers. And when there's one accident, I don't think the answer is to shut down driverless cars. The answer is to say, 'Hey, let's talk about how we prevent more accidents in the future.'" [...] From Langley's answers, it's clear that the ethics around how Flock should be used is a decision he would much rather leave up to others. "We don't want to tell city leaders how to do their job," he noted. "We will provide recommendations, we'll provide defaults, but we're going to minimize the number of mandated features, functions, and policies," he said. Langley went
articles.summary: Flock CEO Langley 在全国舆论反弹中为大规模监控技术辩护，称其有助于提高犯罪追责概率，引发争议。

articles.title: First-Ever Public Confirmation of 'Zero-Click' Spyware Delivered Via Targeted Ads
articles.content: Citizen Lab says it has documented the first publicly confirmed case of zero-click mercenary spyware being delivered through targeted online ads, a technique it calls "AdFection." "There has been a lot of buzz that online ads can be used to identify and automatically hack targets with pinpoint precision, but now for the first time, we have concrete technical evidence showing this process in action," said Bill Marczak, a researcher at Citizen Lab. The Guardian reports: Citizen Lab, a digital investigations research unit at the University of Toronto, said it believed dozens of devices at the Qatari broadcaster Al Jazeera had been compromised by spyware delivered through ads run by Discover-Tech, which describes itself as a specialised digital advertising agency. According to Citizen Lab, Discover-Tech operates a software platform called Controlium that allows its clients to "mass-profile and deanonymize" internet users then covertly hack targets with third-party spyware. Unlike infections that rely on people interacting with links or files, the spyware requires no interaction from the victim to be installed, making it a new delivery technique, Citizen Lab says. The infections happen without a user's knowledge, and in a matter of seconds, according to Citizen Lab. "[The online advertising] ecosystem is being weaponized at a massive scale to profile millions of users, then silently infect targets with zero-click mercenary spyware," the report says. According to the report, Controlium is able to harvest a user's identity and IP address when the user is shown a seemingly benign custom-created ad -- for example, for a digital game or a telecoms service. If the user has been selected as a target for hacking, a mercenary spyware firm can then send a malicious code containing spyware to their device, the researchers say. They say that millions of users worldwide have been served ads by Discover-Tech since 2024, including in Yemen, Brazil, Mexico and Czechia. [...] The full ex
articles.summary: Citizen Lab 首次公开确认通过定向广告投递零点击雇佣间谍软件，将此类攻击手法命名为 AdFection。

articles.title: Microsoft Says Windows 11 Is Now 'More Responsive', Runs Better On 8GB of RAM
articles.content: Microsoft says recent Windows 11 updates have made the operating system up to 20% more responsive by improving memory management and reducing background resource use. "A big part of that work is making smarter use of memory and system resources," says Navjot Virk, corporate vice president of Windows experiences at Microsoft. "We've improved memory management and efficiency across Windows to help keep more of your PC's resources focused on what you're actively doing." The Verge reports: The improvements to memory management now make a "meaningful difference" on PCs with just 8GB of RAM. "Windows can now keep up to 2GB more of your active data in memory instead of moving it to slower storage," says Virk. "For example, on PCs with 8GB of memory or less, Widgets load only when you open them, making more than 200 MB of memory available for your apps and other work." Microsoft has also made Windows Update less disruptive, cleaned up the Widgets section, and finally allowed the taskbar to be repositioned to the sides or top of a display. Windows Hello sign-in has also been sped up, and Bluetooth pairing is more reliable, "including an AirPods pairing experience that's up to 15 seconds faster." The next big step is a new Windows Search experience that's a lot faster and more capable. [...] It's currently available for Windows Insiders, and Microsoft says it will "roll out more broadly later this year." Read more of this story at Slashdot.
articles.summary: 微软称近期 Windows 11 更新通过优化内存管理，使系统响应速度提升最高20%，在8GB内存设备上运行更佳。

articles.title: Amazon Launches New Bee 'Personal AI' Devices That Listen to Conversations
articles.content: Amazon has unveiled two new Bee "personal AI" devices designed to continuously record, transcribe, and analyze conversations: the $75 wearable Bee Frontier and the $100 phone-mounted Bee Eclipse. Amazon says the devices can generate conversation summaries, surface recurring themes, and recommend actions or purchases, while claiming audio itself is never stored and users can delete transcripts and summaries. articles.title: Uber Begins Self-Driving Robotaxi Trial In Manchester
articles.content: An anonymous reader quotes a report from The Guardian: Uber has begun a trial of autonomous vehicles on the streets of Manchester as it looks to bring robotaxis to cities around the UK. The first self-driving cars are operating, using the technology of its partner firms Pony and Verne, with whom Uber recently launched Europe's first autonomous taxi service in the Croatian capital, Zagreb. Uber said it was "excited to take this first step toward making this technology accessible to people across the UK." In social media posts, Verne said it had "started our autonomous vehicle testing in Manchester," while Pony said there were "plans to bring robotaxis to the city" and that testing was under way. The tests involve the company mapping the streets of the city in north-west England with a safety driver behind the wheel and no passengers. Limited passenger services started last month in London, but with a safety driver in the front seat of cars supplied by Wayve under Transport for London's licensing rules for private hire vehicles. The next steps are unclear. Opposition from Uber drivers, their unions and the capital's politicians to the rollout of robotaxis is mounting. The GMB and ADCU unions have both said thousands of drivers jobs will be lost and have called for help for those affected. A critical report from London assembly's transport committee this week called for the government to devolve authority over autonomous taxi services. It said there was "considerable uncertainty about many of the claimed benefits of autonomous passenger vehicles", and fears over the impact on public transport and congestion, as well as safeguarding and accessibility for disabled passengers. There has been no official application to launch passenger services in Manchester so far. Read more of this story at Slashdot.

articles.title: Mutative v2  - better immutability and faster immutable updates
articles.content: Mutative 2.0 is out. Read the release notes , the announcement and the migration guide from v1 to v2 . Mutative - A JavaScript library for efficient immutable updates ( documentation ). In the benchmark , it was about 3.6x faster than Immer with the same settings and 6.6x faster with each library's defaults across 97 workloads. In that benchmark the gap widened on large arrays, where Mutative moved elements up to 1,052x faster than Immer. When copying dominates, such as updating objects with thousands of keys, inserting at the front of a large array or adding an item to a large Set, Mutative is even faster than hand-written reducers. How does Mutative compare with the spread operation (hand-written reducers)? Mutative copies each object at most once per update, however many changes a recipe makes. Immer made it easy to write immutable updates as mutations of a draft. Mutative keeps that model and focuses on performance: it copies each object at most once per update, drafts objects only when a recipe reads them, finalizes only the drafts that changed, and runs array methods that move elements natively on its copies. Immer freezes the next state by default, which costs time on every update; Mutative freezes it only when asked to. Mutative also takes its options per call instead of from global configuration, drafts class instances through marks instead of changing their classes, supports async recipes and Map and Set subclasses, and handles edge cases that Immer gets wrong. Comparison with Immer lists the differences. Mutative passed all of Immer's test cases. Mutative 2.0.0 was 3.6x faster than Immer 11.1.18 with matched settings and 6.6x faster with each library's defaults, on geometric mean across 97 benchmarked workloads, and faster in 595 of 614 measured cases. The gap grows on large arrays, where Mutative moves elements natively: removing the first of 10,000 rows took 7.04 µs, against 7,408 µs. The performance summary has the complete results, the method, and their limits. Its last full run measured 97 of them, and a focused run the two that return fresh data. It compares Mutative with Immer 11.1.18 and with reducers written by hand, after checking every result against those reducers. With matched settings, both libraries freeze or both do not, and both generate patches or both do not. With each library's defaults, Mutative without auto-freeze and Immer with it, Mutative was faster in 154 of 157 cases. The other 3 return a state that Immer froze earlier: Immer skips frozen values when it searches a returned state for drafts, while Mutative, which does not freeze by default, searches it unless the recipe wraps it in rawReturn() , which took 0.26 µs. articles.title: Type-safe OpenAPI requests that follow your document exactly
articles.content: openapi-chain compiles the serialization rules an OpenAPI document declares (parameter style , explode , allowReserved and content , request media types, and form and multipart Encoding Objects) and applies them to every request. A build-time CLI generates types and metadata scoped to the paths you call, so large documents stay affordable to type-check and to ship. Calls use a fluent path API with no generated endpoint code and no runtime dependencies. The pnpm monorepo contains three publishable packages: openapi-chain , @openapi-chain/cli , and @openapi-chain/query . The runtime keeps its existing package name and entry points. See the package migration guide for CLI and query import changes and release availability. The first request below uses the Items schema . Your chain follows your own schema: static path segments become properties, {parameters} become function calls, and HTTP methods become request functions. Exact wire serialization: the strict client sends what the document specifies and rejects representations it cannot encode instead of guessing. The wire comparison executes 20 declarations through both clients: openapi-fetch 0.17.0 sends a request with different values, media type or missing parameters in 16 of them, and differs only in percent-encoding or list spacing in 3 more. Scoped generation for large documents: one CLI config produces full declarations, a path scope and matching runtime metadata. On the pinned GitHub REST document, scoping a 40-operation consumer reduced openapi-chain's TypeScript 7 check time from 0.49 s to 0.045 s ( real-schema measurements ). Typed requests and responses: infer parameters, request media types and status-correlated results from the selected operation. Keep openapi-fetch if you already use it: openapi-chain/openapi-fetch applies the same serialization to an existing openapi-fetch client ( adapter guide ). Small schema-free core: the default client has a 3.5 KiB gzip budget , enforced by a reproducible size check ; its bundle size and per-request overhead are in the same range as openapi-fetch ( client comparison ). Customizable requests: operation-typed extensions and Fetch-compatible transports support application-specific serialization, authentication and parsing. When to choose openapi-chain Choose the strict client when your document declares non-default parameter styles, parameter content , cookie parameters, non-JSON media types or form and multipart encoding, and the server depends on them. Choose the CLI's scoped generation when a large document makes type-checking or metadata delivery expensive. If your API only uses JSON bodies and default parameter styles, openapi-fetch and openapi-chain's core are comparable in size and speed; pick the call style you prefer. Without scoping, openapi-chain's fluent types cost more to check than openapi-fetch's on the measured GitHub and Stripe documents. For a published release with this API: pnpm add openapi-chain pnpm add -D @openapi-chain/cli S

A single command, vp , manages your Node.js runtime, package manager, and frontend toolchain . It is neither a framework, nor a package manager and definitely not a replacement for Vite . Instead, Vite+ ties the tools you already use into one tested stack with a single config file and a consistent set of commands. Vite+ is free, open source under MIT , and framework-agnostic. Whether you ship a React app, a Vue component library, a Node CLI, or a 400-package monorepo, the commands stay the same. Your project does not even have to use Vite in the first place! Starting a web project means a lot of choices to make before even starting to write your first line of code: picking a runtime, choosing a package manager, deciding on a dev server, setting up a linter, a formatter, a test runner, a bundler, you name it. Each one brings its own config files, release cadence, commands, and its own upgrade guide. And that matters for you at least twice . First when you pick the tool stack (or get onboarded to it), then every time things drift apart: the linter disagrees with the formatter, CI runs different commands than you do locally, one repo is two majors behind another, and the person who originally set it up is on vacation. Teams with more than a handful of repositories usually end up building internal scripts to paper over this, which then need their own maintainers. articles.content: Home / Node.js Node.js built-ins that replaced npm packages By Flavio Copes Sep 20, 2026 Twelve Node.js built-ins that replace axios, nodemon, dotenv, jest, chalk, glob and more, with their stability in Node 24 and one gotcha each. ~~~ Open a package.json from a few years ago and you’ll find the same names in almost every one. axios , nodemon , dotenv , jest , chalk , uuid , rimraf . Node.js now ships a built-in for each of them. Here are twelve of those built-ins, with the package each one replaces, the shortest example that runs, how stable it is in the current LTS line, and the one thing the old package still does that the built-in doesn’t. Several of these changed status in the last year, so I checked every claim against the Node 24 API docs (24.21.0, the Active LTS line as of September 2026) and ran every example on Node 26.0.0, which is what node --version prints on my Mac. Node 22 is in maintenance until April 2027, Node 20 reached end of life on April 30, 2026, and Node 26 becomes the next LTS on October 28, 2026. Where Node 22 and 24 differ, I say so. A quick reminder on how Node labels its APIs. Stability 2 is stable. Stability 1 is experimental, with sub-levels: 1.0 is early development, 1.1 is active development, 1.2 is a release candidate. Anything experimental can change or disappear in a minor release, so the number matters if you’re putting it in production. 1. node:sqlite replaces better-sqlite3 For years the way to use SQLite from Node was better-sqlite3 , a native addon you had to compile (or download a prebuilt binary for) on every install. Node 22.5 added a SQLite driver to core. Like better-sqlite3 , it’s synchronous, so the code reads top to bottom with no await . import { DatabaseSync } from 'node:sqlite' const db = new DatabaseSync ( '/Users/flavio/notes.db' ) db. exec ( 'CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS notes (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, body TEXT)' ) const insert = db. prepare ( 'INSERT INTO notes (body) VALUES (?)' ) insert. run ( 'Buy espresso beans' ) console. log (db. prepare ( 'SELECT * FROM notes' ). all ()) The module only exists under the node: prefix, a plain import 'sqlite' fails. Status in Node 24: 1.2, release candidate , since 24.15.0. It prints no warning. In Node 22 it’s still 1.1, active development (the --experimental-sqlite flag went away in 22.13, the label didn’t), so a server on Node 22 is running an API the docs describe as “nearing minimum viability”. Where it does less: better-sqlite3 has db.transaction(fn) , which wraps a function in BEGIN , COMMIT and ROLLBACK for you, and node:sqlite has nothing like it. You write those three statements yourself in a try / catch . I show the pattern in node:sqlite: SQLite built into Node.js , and the free SQLite course covers transactions and indexes in more depth. 2. node:test and node:assert replace Jest and Mocha Jest was the default test runner for a long time, and I have a whole post on it from 2018. articles.title: Tibetan-Singing-Bowls: Strike or rub a set of virtual Tibetan singing bowls - synthesized in the browser with Web Audio, with the beating overtones of the real thing
articles.content: Play a set of virtual Tibetan singing bowls right in your browser. Strike a bowl, or hold it down to draw the tone out the way a mallet circles the rim. The sound is synthesized live, so there are no audio files to load, and it works offline. Use headphones or good speakers. Seven bowls are tuned to a scale, each with its own color. Tap or click a bowl to strike it. Switch to Sing and hold a bowl down to make it swell and sustain, then let go to let it fade. The number keys 1 to 7 play the bowls from the keyboard, and you can play several at once. Tuning : a seven-note chakra scale (C to B, one bowl per chakra) or a pentatonic scale, in the low, middle or high octave, with A at 440 Hz or 432 Hz. Sound : volume and room reverb. Spectrum : a live view of the sound, so you can watch the overtones rise and fade. Sound bath : press start and pick 5, 10, 20 or 30 minutes, and the bowls play by themselves, one strike at a time, with silence in between. A struck bowl rings at its fundamental plus overtones at about 2.7, 5.2 and 8.3 times that pitch. Those overtones are not whole-number multiples, which is why a bowl sounds like a bell and not like a string. Each partial is made of two sine oscillators a fraction of a hertz apart, so it swells and fades a few times a second: that beating is the "wah-wah" of a real bowl. Higher partials die away faster. The result goes through a synthesized room reverb and a compressor. This is a model of the sound and not a recording. The bowls are not meant as a medical treatment, and the chakra colors are a common convention, not a measurement. The pages are plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript with the Web Audio API, with no dependencies and no build step. Just open index.html . It is also a small installable web app: add it to your home screen or desktop and it works offline. The bowls are drawn as SVG. The app logic is in js/bowls.js . Three color themes (dark, light and blue) are shared with my other projects. Your tuning, volume and other settings are kept in the browser's local storage. Tibetan-Singing-Bowls is open source at GitHub with MIT license. Had fun browsing the app? Buy me a coffee by becoming a sponsor . You may also be interested in my other sound projects Crystal-Singing-Bowls ( demo ), Healing-Frequencies ( demo ) and Cymatics ( demo ). For more mystic arts as small web apps, see Esoterica . Strokes are stored in normalized coordinates, so the drawing stays the same when the window is resized. The canvas is redrawn from the stroke list, with an offscreen cache for speed. The SVG export writes each stroke once and repeats it with use elements. The app logic is in js/mandala.js . Three color themes (dark, light and blue) are shared with my other projects. There is also an About mandalas page on what mandalas are, where they come from (Hindu and Buddhist traditions, Jung), and what research does and does not say about their effect on the mind.
